questions.stem: A 44 year old woman with a BMI of 33 and four children has 36 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain that began after a fried meal. It radiates to her right shoulder. She has vomited twice. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. She catches her breath when the right upper quadrant is pressed during deep inspiration. The site of pain is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Where the pain is
visual.caption: Right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Constant RUQ pain radiating to the shoulder with fever and a positive Murphy's sign in a '4 F' patient is acute cholecystitis. Biliary colic has no fever.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Female, fat, forty, fertile; constant RUQ pain with fever and a positive Murphy's sign.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute cholecystitis.

elim: Pain is epigastric radiating to the back, not RUQ to the shoulder.
Gives jaundice and very high transaminases, with no Murphy's sign.
No fever and pain settles within hours.
Can cause RUQ pain but would give cough and chest signs.

steps.x: **A. Acute cholecystitis.** Constant RUQ pain + fever + Murphy's sign = acute cholecystitis.

questions.stem:
A 47 year old woman with known gallstones has had right upper quadrant pain for 20 hours. Previous attacks lasted 2 hours and settled on their own, but this one has not. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg. She is not jaundiced.

Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Persistent pain with fever and raised CRP and WCC means a stone has stayed impacted in the cystic duct, causing cholecystitis. Biliary colic has normal markers.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Pain over 6 hours with fever and raised WCC/CRP means inflammation, not just colic. Normal bilirubin argues against a duct stone.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute cholecystitis.

elim: Amylase is normal.
Needs jaundice; her bilirubin is normal.
Biliary colic has no fever and normal inflammatory markers.
Would give an obstructive LFT pattern with raised bilirubin.

steps.x: **A. Acute cholecystitis.** Biliary colic + fever + raised inflammatory markers = cholecystitis.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman who is 26 weeks pregnant has 2 days of constant right upper quadrant pain, nausea and vomiting. She has had similar shorter pains after meals in the past. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg and urinalysis shows no protein. Her ALT is 48 U/L (<40) and platelets 260 × 10⁹/L (150–400).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fertility and pregnancy increase gallstone risk, and constant RUQ pain with fever is acute cholecystitis. Normal BP, no proteinuria and normal platelets exclude pre-eclampsia and HELLP.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Pregnancy ('fertile') raises gallstone risk; fever and constant RUQ pain point to cholecystitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute cholecystitis.

elim: Can move upwards in pregnancy, but previous post-prandial RUQ pains suggest gallstones.
Occurs in the third trimester with liver failure and hypoglycaemia.
Needs hypertension, haemolysis and low platelets.
Her BP is normal and there is no proteinuria.

steps.x: **B. Acute cholecystitis.** Pregnancy is a gallstone risk factor; normal BP and platelets exclude HELLP and pre-eclampsia.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman has constant right upper quadrant pain for 2 days with a temperature of 38.1°C. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 126/82 mmHg. There is right upper quadrant tenderness. Ultrasound shows gallstones with a thickened gallbladder wall. She describes the pain spreading to another site.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of radiation of her pain?
questions.e: Acute cholecystitis pain typically radiates to the right shoulder or scapula. Back pain is more typical of pancreatitis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Gallbladder inflammation irritates the diaphragm and refers to the right shoulder or scapula.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Right shoulder tip (or right scapula).

elim: Typical of ureteric colic.
Suggests splenic or left subdiaphragmatic irritation.
More typical of pancreatitis or an aortic aneurysm.
Early appendicitis pain starts here.

steps.x: **D. Right shoulder tip.** Cholecystitis pain radiates to the right shoulder/scapula.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has 2 days of right upper quadrant pain and fever. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. Pressing below the right costal margin during deep inspiration makes her stop breathing in because of pain. A student wants to confirm the sign is specific.
questions.q: Which finding makes this sign specific for acute cholecystitis?
o: No pain with the same manoeuvre on the left
Pain on releasing pressure in the right iliac fossa
Pain on the right that also occurs on the left
questions.e: Murphy's sign is positive when pressing the RUQ during deep inspiration halts inspiration, and it is only specific if negative on the left.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: stop breathing in because of pain
steps.x: Murphy's sign is only specific if the same test on the left does not cause pain.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Negative on the left side.

elim: Rebound tenderness; not specific for the gallbladder.
Bilateral pain makes the sign non-specific.
A non-specific sign of peritonism.
Suggests generalised peritonitis.

steps.x: **A. No pain with the same manoeuvre on the left.** Murphy's sign: RUQ pain halts inspiration, and the same test on the left must be negative.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with type 2 diabetes has been treated for 3 days with IV antibiotics for acute cholecystitis. He suddenly develops severe generalised abdominal pain. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 128 bpm and BP 88/54 mmHg. His abdomen is rigid with guarding in all quadrants and absent bowel sounds.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sustained inflammation can cause gallbladder wall ischaemia, gangrene and perforation, giving sudden generalised peritonitis and sepsis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: suddenly develops severe generalised abdominal pain
rigid with guarding in all quadrants
steps.x: Sustained inflammation causes wall ischaemia and gangrene; sudden generalised peritonitis means the gallbladder has perforated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gallbladder perforation with biliary peritonitis.

elim: Does not usually cause sudden generalised rigidity.
Gives jaundice and rigors, not generalised peritonitis.
Self-limiting pain without fever or shock.
Pain out of proportion to signs, not a rigid abdomen from the start.

steps.x: **D. Gallbladder perforation.** Cholecystitis + sudden generalised peritonitis = perforation.

questions.stem: An 82 year old woman from a care home has acute cholecystitis. She has become drowsy and confused over 6 hours. Her temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Her lactate is 4.6 mmol/L (<2.0). Her abdomen is tender only in the right upper quadrant.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Hypotension, confusion and a raised lactate with localised RUQ tenderness indicate sepsis from cholecystitis. Perforation would cause generalised peritonitis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: tender only in the right upper quadrant
steps.x: Hypotension, confusion and a raised lactate with a localised RUQ source is sepsis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Sepsis secondary to acute cholecystitis.

elim: Confusion here comes with shock and a high lactate, not focal signs.
Tenderness is limited to the RUQ, not generalised.
Would not explain the fever and raised lactate.
There is a clear abdominal source already.

steps.x: **D. Sepsis from acute cholecystitis.** Complications of cholecystitis: sepsis, empyema, perforation, peritonitis.

questions.stem: A 53 year old woman had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy 5 months ago. She now has colicky upper abdominal pain, loose stools and is newly jaundiced. Her temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. Her wound sites are healed and she has no drain.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Colicky pain, diarrhoea and new jaundice months after cholecystectomy is post-cholecystectomy syndrome. A bile leak appears within days.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: colicky upper abdominal pain, loose stools
steps.x: Colicky pain, diarrhoea and new jaundice months after cholecystectomy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Post-cholecystectomy syndrome.

elim: Presents in the first days after surgery with bile in the drain.
No risk factors, and the symptoms follow cholecystectomy.
Does not cause jaundice.
Cause obstruction, not jaundice and diarrhoea.

steps.x: **D. Post-cholecystectomy syndrome.** Post-cholecystectomy syndrome: colicky pain, diarrhoea, new jaundice after cholecystectomy.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy 2 days ago. Her drain now contains green fluid and she has right upper quadrant pain. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. Her ALP and bilirubin are mildly raised. MRCP shows normal calibre ducts with no stones and contrast escaping from the cystic duct remnant.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause?
o: Missed distal common bile duct stone
Slipped clip on the cystic duct stump
questions.e: Bile in the drain with a leak from the cystic duct remnant and no CBD stone is most likely from a slipped clip. Duct injury would show the leak from the common hepatic or bile duct.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Bile in the drain = bile leak. A leak from the cystic duct remnant with clear ducts is a slipped clip.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Slipped cystic duct clip.

elim: Would leak enteric content and gas, not from the cystic duct.
MRCP shows no stones.
Occurs weeks to months later without bile in a drain.
The leak is from the cystic duct remnant, and the ducts are intact.

steps.x: **D. Slipped clip on the cystic duct stump.** Bile leak causes: slipped clips, missed distal CBD stone, or iatrogenic duct injury.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with diabetes has 3 days of fever and right upper quadrant pain. He is not jaundiced. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 106 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a stone in the neck of the gallbladder, a thickened gallbladder wall and pericholecystic fluid. The common bile duct is 5 mm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A stone obstructing the cystic duct with wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid and fever is acute cholecystitis. A normal duct without jaundice argues against cholangitis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: stone in the neck of the gallbladder
steps.x: A stone at the gallbladder neck obstructing the cystic duct, wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid with fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute cholecystitis.

elim: No jaundice and a normal calibre common bile duct.
No fever or wall thickening in uncomplicated colic.
Presents with weight loss and a mass, not acute fever.
Ultrasound would show a hepatic collection.

steps.x: **A. Acute cholecystitis.** Ultrasound triad of cholecystitis: stones, wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has 5 days of right upper quadrant pain treated with oral antibiotics by her GP. She now has a high fever with rigors and a tender, palpable right upper quadrant mass. Her temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 104/64 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a distended gallbladder full of echogenic fluid.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A distended gallbladder full of pus with high fever and a tender RUQ mass is an empyema. A mucocoele is distended but not infected.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: tender, palpable right upper quadrant mass
steps.x: An obstructed, infected gallbladder full of pus: high fever, tender mass and echogenic contents.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gallbladder empyema.

elim: No fever or mass.
Painless and non-tender, without fever.
Not an acute febrile presentation.
Distended but not infected or febrile.

steps.x: **C. Gallbladder empyema.** Cholecystitis not settling + swinging fever + tender RUQ mass = empyema.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has 2 days of constant right upper quadrant pain that began after a takeaway meal. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. Her bilirubin is 15 µmol/L (<21) and CRP 118 mg/L (<5). Ultrasound shows stones in the gallbladder. A student asks what has caused her illness.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her illness?
o: Bacterial infection ascending from the duodenum into the CBD
Impacted stone blocking the cystic duct
Stone obstructing the ampulla of Vater
questions.e: Acute cholecystitis is caused by a gallstone obstructing the cystic duct. A stone at the ampulla causes pancreatitis or jaundice.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Cholecystitis is gallbladder inflammation caused by a stone obstructing the cystic duct.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gallstone impacted in the cystic duct.

elim: Describes cholangitis; her bilirubin is normal.
Can cause acalculous disease, but stones are present.
Would cause pancreatitis or obstructive jaundice.
Would raise transaminases and bilirubin.

steps.x: **C. Impacted stone blocking the cystic duct.** Cholecystitis = cystic duct; cholangitis = common bile duct; pancreatitis = ampulla.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has 30 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain and vomiting. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 134/84 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. He winces on deep inspiration while the right upper quadrant is palpated. His chest is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial imaging investigation?
questions.e: Abdominal ultrasound is the most appropriate first-line investigation for cholecystitis. Abdominal X-ray misses most gallstones.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
Suspected acute cholecystitis: first test is ultrasound.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Abdominal ultrasound.

elim: Most gallstones are not radio-opaque.
Second-line if the diagnosis is unclear or complications are suspected.
Therapeutic and invasive; not diagnostic for cholecystitis.
Used to image the bile ducts, not first line for cholecystitis.

steps.x: **A. Abdominal ultrasound.** Suspected cholecystitis: ultrasound first.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman has had recurrent biliary colic for a year. She now has 2 days of constant right upper quadrant pain with a temperature of 38.3°C. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. An abdominal ultrasound is performed.
questions.q: Which ultrasound finding best supports acute cholecystitis rather than biliary colic?
o: Contracted gallbladder with a normal wall
questions.e: Gallstones occur in both conditions; wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid show the inflammation of cholecystitis.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
Stones are seen in both; inflammation shows as wall thickening (and pericholecystic fluid).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gallbladder wall thickening.

elim: Suggests chronic disease or a post-meal scan.
Suggests duct obstruction, not cholecystitis.
Present in both biliary colic and cholecystitis.
Expected in both; it does not distinguish them.

steps.x: **E. Thickened gallbladder wall.** Biliary colic: stones, normal wall. Cholecystitis: stones, thick wall, pericholecystic fluid.

questions.stem: A 43 year old woman has 2 days of constant right upper quadrant pain, fever and vomiting. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. Murphy's sign is positive. Ultrasound confirms acute cholecystitis without bile duct dilatation. Blood tests are sent.
questions.q: Which set of blood results is most likely?
o: Amylase over 3 times the upper limit
Bilirubin 140 µmol/L with markedly raised ALP
Raised CRP and WCC with mildly abnormal LFTs
questions.e: The inflammatory response in cholecystitis raises CRP and WCC, and LFTs may be mildly abnormal. Normal inflammatory markers suggest biliary colic.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
Inflammation raises CRP and WCC; LFTs may be mildly abnormal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Raised CRP and WCC, mildly abnormal LFTs.

elim: Suggests pancreatitis.
Suggests CBD obstruction, but the duct is not dilated.
Seen in uncomplicated biliary colic.
Suggests hepatitis or ischaemic liver injury.

steps.x: **D. Raised CRP and WCC with mildly abnormal LFTs.** Cholecystitis bloods: raised CRP and WCC, abnormal LFTs. Normal markers = biliary colic.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant has constant right upper quadrant pain and a temperature of 38.0°C. Her pulse rate is 100 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg. Murphy's sign is positive. She is worried about radiation exposure to her baby.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Ultrasound is the first-line test for cholecystitis and has no radiation, so it is safe in pregnancy.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
Ultrasound is first line and is radiation-free, so it is ideal in pregnancy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Abdominal ultrasound.

elim: Uses radiation and misses most stones.
Uses radiation; not first line.
Invasive, uses radiation and is not diagnostic for cholecystitis.
Uses radioisotopes; not first line.

steps.x: **A. Abdominal ultrasound.** Ultrasound first for cholecystitis, including in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has 4 hours of colicky right upper quadrant pain after a meal, which has now settled. She is afebrile. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. Ultrasound shows gallstones with a normal gallbladder wall. A doctor wants to know whether she has cholecystitis.
questions.q: Which investigation best helps exclude acute cholecystitis?
questions.e: Cholecystitis raises CRP and WCC; normal markers with a normal wall support uncomplicated biliary colic.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation: think what answers the clinical question right now.
Cholecystitis raises inflammatory markers; normal CRP and WCC with a normal wall favour biliary colic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: CRP and WCC.

elim: A tumour marker, not useful here.
Does not assess inflammation.
Tests for pancreatitis, not cholecystitis.
Not relevant to gallbladder inflammation.

steps.x: **B. CRP and white cell count.** Raised CRP and WCC separate cholecystitis from biliary colic.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has 2 days of constant right upper quadrant pain and vomiting. Her temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. Her mucous membranes are dry. Ultrasound confirms acute cholecystitis. She has no allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IV fluids, analgesia and IV antibiotics
questions.e: Initial management is IV fluids, analgesia and IV antibiotics, followed by early laparoscopic cholecystectomy. ERCP is for duct stones.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Dehydrated and septic-looking: resuscitate, control pain and give IV antibiotics.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: IV fluids, analgesia and IV antibiotics.

elim: She is vomiting, febrile and tachycardic; she needs admission.
Initial management is medical; surgery is laparoscopic and planned early.
Treats biliary colic, not cholecystitis.
For bile duct stones or cholangitis, not cholecystitis.

steps.x: **C. IV fluids, analgesia and IV antibiotics.** Cholecystitis first line: IV fluids, analgesia, IV antibiotics (co-amoxiclav).

questions.stem: A 48 year old man has acute cholecystitis confirmed on ultrasound. He has no drug allergies and normal renal function. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. He has received IV fluids and analgesia. The team now prescribes an antibiotic.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: IV co-amoxiclav covers enteric organisms such as E. coli. Cefuroxime plus metronidazole is used if penicillin allergic.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Cover enteric organisms such as E. coli with IV co-amoxiclav.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: IV co-amoxiclav.

elim: For MRSA or C. difficile, not enteric Gram-negatives.
Respiratory macrolide; poor cover for E. coli.
Only works in the urinary tract.
Narrow streptococcal cover.

steps.x: **A. IV co-amoxiclav.** Cholecystitis: IV co-amoxiclav; if penicillin-allergic, cefuroxime plus metronidazole.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman is admitted with acute cholecystitis diagnosed on ultrasound 12 hours ago. She is otherwise fit and well. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. She is responding to IV antibiotics. The surgical team discuss the timing of surgery.
questions.q: When is laparoscopic cholecystectomy best performed?
o: Only if symptoms recur within a year
questions.e: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, ideally within 72 hours and within 1 week, is preferred over delayed interval surgery (NICE and Tokyo guidance).

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy is preferred, ideally within 72 hours and within 1 week.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Within 72 hours.

elim: Delayed surgery risks recurrent attacks; early surgery is preferred.
Recurrence is common; surgery is offered after the first.
Not recommended practice.
Too delayed.

steps.x: **B. Ideally within 72 hours of presentation.** Cholecystitis: early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, ideally ≤72 hours, within 1 week.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman's acute cholecystitis has settled after 48 hours of IV antibiotics. She is fit with no comorbidities. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg. She wants to avoid having another attack.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the definitive treatment and prevents future episodes. Cholecystostomy is for patients unfit for surgery.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Removing the gallbladder is the definitive treatment and prevents further episodes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

elim: Treats bile duct stones, not the gallbladder.
Not used for gallstones in the UK.
Rarely dissolves stones and does not prevent attacks reliably.
A drainage procedure for patients unfit for surgery.

steps.x: **C. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy.** Definitive treatment of cholecystitis = early laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has a gallbladder empyema. After 72 hours of IV co-amoxiclav he is worse, with swinging fevers. His temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 122 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a tense, distended gallbladder full of echogenic fluid.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue IV antibiotics and review in a week
questions.e: A gallbladder empyema that deteriorates on antibiotics needs urgent drainage by percutaneous cholecystostomy or surgery.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.

clues: After 72 hours of IV co-amoxiclav he is worse
steps.x: An empyema that worsens despite antibiotics needs source control.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urgent percutaneous cholecystostomy or surgical drainage.

elim: He is deteriorating; this is less treatment, not more.
Pus needs draining; waiting risks perforation.
Too late for an empyema that is getting worse.
Does not drain the gallbladder.

steps.x: **E. Urgent drainage of the gallbladder.** Empyema deteriorating despite antibiotics = urgent cholecystostomy or surgical drainage.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy 3 days ago. Her drain is producing 300 mL of bile a day and she has right upper quadrant pain. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. Her LFTs are abnormal. MRCP shows a leak from the cystic duct stump.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: A bile leak is managed with ERCP, which lowers biliary pressure so the leak can seal.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.

clues: leak from the cystic duct stump
steps.x: A bile leak is managed by ERCP (stent or sphincterotomy) to lower duct pressure so the leak seals.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: ERCP.

elim: Grossly inappropriate.
The leak would collect as a biloma.
The gallbladder has already been removed.
Does not seal a leak.

steps.x: **B. ERCP.** Bile leak after cholecystectomy is managed with ERCP.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has acute cholecystitis. On day 2 she develops sudden severe generalised abdominal pain. Her temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 126 bpm and BP 90/56 mmHg. Her abdomen is rigid throughout. CT shows free fluid and a defect in the gallbladder wall. IV fluids and antibiotics have been started.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Gallbladder perforation with peritonitis needs resuscitation, antibiotics and emergency surgery. Antibiotics alone do not control the source.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide how sick the patient is and what changes the outcome next.
Perforation with generalised peritonitis needs urgent surgical source control.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Emergency surgery (cholecystectomy and washout).

elim: Perforation with peritonitis needs source control.
Far too late for peritonitis.
Does not treat a perforated gallbladder.
She has septic shock from peritonitis.

steps.x: **C. Emergency surgery.** Perforated gallbladder with peritonitis = resuscitate, antibiotics, emergency surgery.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has had biliary colic before, which always settled within 2 hours. This attack has lasted 2 days with constant right upper quadrant pain and fever. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a distended gallbladder with a thickened wall.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this attack?
o: Gallbladder wall spasm from a stone moving out of the duct
Persistent cystic duct obstruction causing bile stasis and wall inflammation
Primary viral infection of the gallbladder
Reflux of pancreatic enzymes into the gallbladder
Stone obstructing the common bile duct
questions.e: Persistent cystic duct obstruction prevents emptying, causing bile stasis, wall distension and mucosal inflammation. Transient obstruction gives biliary colic.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.

clues: distended gallbladder with a thickened wall
steps.x: A stone that stays in the cystic duct stops the gallbladder emptying, causing bile stasis, distension and inflammation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Persistent cystic duct obstruction with bile stasis and inflammation.

elim: Describes biliary colic, which is transient.
Infection is secondary, after obstruction.
Not the mechanism of cholecystitis.
Would cause jaundice.

steps.x: **B. Persistent cystic duct obstruction causing bile stasis and wall inflammation.** Colic = transient obstruction; cholecystitis = persistent obstruction → stasis → inflammation.

questions.stem: A 51 year old woman has acute cholecystitis. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 106 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Blood cultures grow a Gram-negative bacillus that ferments lactose. A student asks where the organism came from.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Secondary bacterial infection in cholecystitis is usually from enteric organisms, most commonly E. coli, a lactose-fermenting Gram-negative bacillus.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the vignette to the underlying process.
Secondary infection of the obstructed gallbladder is by enteric organisms; a lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod is E. coli.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Escherichia coli.

elim: Gram-negative but non-lactose fermenting; a hospital organism.
Non-lactose fermenter; causes enteric fever.
Gram-positive coccus.
Gram-positive diplococcus causing pneumonia.

steps.x: **A. Escherichia coli.** Cholecystitis infection is secondary and enteric, most commonly E. coli.
